questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=x-{x}^{4}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=1.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x-{x}^{4})=1-4{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{4})\sqrt{1+{(1-4{x}^{3})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{4})\sqrt{2-8{x}^{3}+16{x}^{6}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve $y=2x-{x}^{2}$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $x$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $x$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-{x}^{2} & =0 \\ x(2-x) & =0 \\ x & =0,2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $x=0$ to $x=2.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x-{x}^{2})=2-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-{x}^{2})\sqrt{1+{(2-2x)}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-{x}^{2})\sqrt{5-8x+4{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $x=\sqrt{y}$ that lies between $y=1$ and $y=4.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${y}_{1}=1$ to ${y}_{2}=4.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\sqrt{y})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}y\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}y\sqrt{\frac{4y+1}{y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\pi {\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{y(4y+1)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the arc of the curve $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ that lies in the first quadrant between its $y$-intercepts (see figure above). What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis?
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x=f(y),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =\pm n\pi ,\,n\in Z\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=\pi .$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{\pi }y\sqrt{1+{cos}^{2}⁡y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=1.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}})=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{{x}^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}1\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi x\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2\pi (1-0) \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2}$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=3.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S=\int 2\pi y\,\text{d}s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y=f(x),$ we have 

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from ${x}_{1}=0$ to ${x}_{2}=3.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})=\frac{1-x}{2\sqrt{x}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{1-2x+{x}^{2}}{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})\sqrt{1+\frac{1-2x+{x}^{2}}{4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}(\sqrt{x}-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3/2})\sqrt{\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{4x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{\sqrt{x}(3-x)}{3}(\frac{x+1}{2\sqrt{x}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}(3-x)(x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}(3+2x-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\pi {[3x+{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot 9 \\  & =3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=e^x$ that lies between the lines $x=0$ and $x=2.$ What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y = f(x),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $x_1=0$ to $x_2={2}.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{x})={e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{x}\sqrt{1+({e}^{x})^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{x}\sqrt{1+{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the arc of the curve $x=y^3-y$ that lies in the second quadrant between its $y$-intercepts. What integral gives the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131010/assets/1bdbe21cbb517645dfe9362f3313c2d85118acfea1d839fe33ae9b9ac6c3ed50.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $x = f(y),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d y}\right)^2}\,\textrm d y.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{y_1}^{y_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}y.
$$

First, we need to determine the limits of integration. To do this, we find where the curve intersects the $y$-axis by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3}-y & =0 \\ y({y}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm 1\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we need to integrate from $y=0$ to $y=1.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}({y}^{3}-y)=3{y}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{y}_{1}}^{{y}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{1+{(3{y}^{2}-1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}y\sqrt{2-6{y}^{2}+9{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the arc of the curve $y=\sqrt{x-2}$ that lies between the lines $x=2$ and $x=4.$ Calculate the surface area generated when this arc is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can find the surface area generated when a curve is rotated $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis using the formula

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s.
$$

Since we're given a curve in the form $y = f(x),$ we have 

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we will use

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

We are told that the limits of integration are from $x_1=2$ to $x_2=4.$ 

Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x-2})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x-2}}\,⇒\,{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}=\frac{1}{4(x-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{x-2}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{4(x-2)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{x-2}\sqrt{\frac{4x-7}{4(x-2)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{x-2}(\frac{\sqrt{4x-7}}{2\sqrt{x-2}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{4x-7}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the substitution 

$$
u=4x-7 \quad \Rightarrow\quad \textrm du = 4\,\textrm dx,
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =\pi {\int }_{2}^{4}\sqrt{4x-7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3}{\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,|}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the arc of the curve $y=f(x)$ that lies between the vertical lines $x=x_1$ and $x=x_2,$ as shown below on the left. By rotating this curve $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a **surface of revolution,** as shown below on the right. How can we find its surface area?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131010/assets/d929311a1d86da82fd2acb517ed148715273d37a66928f0cb2949353e06457e1.png)

First, we divide the interval $[a,b]$ into small subintervals, each of length $\Delta{x}.$ Let's consider a part of the curve that corresponds to one of those subintervals and let the length of the corresponding curved arc be $\Delta{s}.$ When this part of the curve is rotated about the $x$-axis, it forms a closed strip. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131010/assets/55ff01b354818b7ec3b9240d470acfa14c648b967f142b7554c172d12e2ca57b.png)

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can assume that both left and right radii of the strip are approximately equal to $y=f(x).$ Then, this strip can be viewed as the lateral surface of a right cylinder with height $h=\Delta{s}$ and radius $r=y=f(x).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131010/assets/5a71ce7729d37ca3d1fb86067f0d3f2233243a24710d08132dfc63f372bb6521.png)

We can approximate the lateral surface area of such a cylinder as

$$
S_{\text{strip}} \approx S_{\text{cylinder}} = 2\pi r \cdot h = 2\pi y \cdot \Delta{s}.
$$

The sum over all subintervals will approximate the total area $S$ that we want. The approximation becomes more and more accurate as $\Delta{s} \to 0$. Therefore, to get the area of the surface, we need to integrate:

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s
$$

Recall that for a curve $y = f(x),$ the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we can find the total surface area using the formula

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.
$$

Consider the arc of the curve $y=f(x)$ that lies between the vertical lines $x=x_1$ and $x=x_2,$ as shown below on the left. By rotating this curve $2\pi$ radians about the $x$-axis, we get a **surface of revolution,** as shown below on the right. How can we find its surface area?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131010/assets/d929311a1d86da82fd2acb517ed148715273d37a66928f0cb2949353e06457e1.png)

First, we divide the interval $[a,b]$ into small subintervals, each of length $\Delta{x}.$ Let's consider a part of the curve that corresponds to one of those subintervals and let the length of the corresponding curved arc be $\Delta{s}.$ When this part of the curve is rotated about the $x$-axis, it forms a closed strip. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131010/assets/55ff01b354818b7ec3b9240d470acfa14c648b967f142b7554c172d12e2ca57b.png)

If $\Delta{x}$ is very small, we can assume that both left and right radii of the strip are approximately equal to $y=f(x).$ Then, this strip can be viewed as the lateral surface of a right cylinder with height $h=\Delta{s}$ and radius $r=y=f(x).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14131010/assets/5a71ce7729d37ca3d1fb86067f0d3f2233243a24710d08132dfc63f372bb6521.png)

We can approximate the lateral surface area of such a cylinder as

$$
S_{\text{strip}} \approx S_{\text{cylinder}} = 2\pi r \cdot h = 2\pi y \cdot \Delta{s}.
$$

The sum over all subintervals will approximate the total area $S$ that we want. The approximation becomes more and more accurate as $\Delta{s} \to 0$. Therefore, to get the area of the surface, we need to integrate:

$$
S = \int 2\pi y\,\textrm d s
$$

Recall that for a curve $y = f(x),$ the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

$$
\textrm d s = \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}\right)^2}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Therefore, we can find the total surface area using the formula

$$
S = 2\pi \int_{x_1}^{x_2} y \sqrt{1+ \left( \dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \right)^2} \: \textrm{d}x.
$$
